title: Delhi High Court Seeks FSSAI Reply on Analogue Products Sold as Paneer
excerpt: A bench gave the Centre, FSSAI and Delhi government six weeks to respond to a PIL targeting non-dairy substitutes passed off as paneer without disclosure, while declining interim enforcement directions.
body:
• The Delhi High Court has sought replies in six weeks from the Centre, FSSAI, the Delhi government and the Commissioner of Food Safety on a PIL against non-dairy products being sold or served as paneer.
  • The plea by law student Ridhima Singh and advocate Avlokiteshwar Padmapani Sidharth does not seek a blanket ban on lawful analogues — it targets products passed off as paneer without disclosure.
  • The court declined interim directions for an enforcement drive, noting authorities said they were already acting and had placed statistics before it.
  • Reader check: FSSAI's September 24 draft amendment would bar the word paneer for products made of non-milk constituents — until rules change, ask restaurants and sellers whether paneer is dairy or analogue.

The Delhi High Court has sought responses from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the Centre, the Delhi government and the Commissioner of Food Safety on a public interest litigation seeking action against dairy analogues and non-dairy products being sold or served as paneer in the capital.

A division bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma directed the authorities to file replies in six weeks, according to Bar and Bench and Verdictum. The court declined to pass interim directions for an immediate enforcement drive.

What the Petition Actually Asks For

The PIL, Ridhima Singh and Another v Union of India and Others, was filed by law student Ridhima Singh and advocate Avlokiteshwar Padmapani Sidharth. It asks the Delhi government and food safety authorities to carry out regular inspections, sampling and testing of paneer at manufacturing units, wholesale markets, distributors, retail outlets and food service establishments, and to require clear disclosure when hotels, restaurants, caterers, cloud kitchens and e-commerce food businesses use analogue substitutes.

The petitioners are explicit about the limit of their case: it does not seek a blanket prohibition on lawful plant-based or dairy analogue products. The target is substitution without disclosure. As the plea puts it, a consumer who knowingly buys a correctly disclosed analogue makes an informed choice, but a consumer who orders paneer "is entitled to receive a product which answers the statutory description of paneer" and should not unknowingly be supplied a product in which milk constituents have been replaced by vegetable fat, vegetable oil or other non-milk ingredients.

"A consumer who purchases or orders 'paneer' is entitled to receive a product which answers the statutory description of paneer and ought not to be unknowingly supplied a product in which essential milk constituents have been substituted."

— Petition in Ridhima Singh v Union of India, as reported by Verdictum

Why Paneer, and Why Now

Paneer is a standardised dairy product under the food safety regime, while an analogue is made to look, feel and function like paneer with some or all milk constituents replaced. Petitioners' counsel told the court, as reported by LawStreet Journal, that a person ordering paneer tikka, kadai paneer or paneer butter masala has no way of knowing whether a restaurant or cloud kitchen used a substitute — "it can be a replicate, it looks and tastes like paneer, there is no disclosure" — and pointed to the Food Safety and Standards Regulations, 2011, arguing paneer is protein-rich while analogues were described in court as largely carbohydrates. The plea also links the consumer's right to food matching its description to the right to health under Article 21, as summarised by Hindustan Times via Kokthum.

The petitioners cited the festive season in seeking urgent sampling. The bench did not grant interim relief, responding that authorities were already acting: "They are doing it, they have placed the statistics (before us) to that effect." Delhi counsel Sameer Vashisth said the government acts as soon as instances come to notice. The plea cites an August 2026 action at Okhla Sabzi Mandi that reportedly destroyed about 508 kg of suspected spurious paneer, and steps taken in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab and Chhattisgarh.

The FSSAI Rule Change Already in Motion

The case runs parallel to a regulatory change. FSSAI's draft amendment, published September 24, would add "paneer made of constituents not derived from milk" to the prohibited list, and "Analogue in Dairy Context" products would have to drop the word paneer from name, labelling and marketing. Petitioners argue authorities need not wait — the existing Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 already allows action, as other states have shown.

What's Next

The Centre, FSSAI, Delhi government and food safety commissioner have six weeks to reply. For consumers, the practical position until then is disclosure, not assumption: check packaged products for "analogue" labelling. The High Court's next hearing will test whether the authorities' statistics satisfy the bench or whether court-directed inspections and disclosure rules follow.
